content_blocks.content:
Sandwich Ontology
1 Introduction
A sandwich is simply bread plus filling, yet even Simple English Wikipedia lists open-faced,
toasted, double-decker, and panini—variants defined by slice and layer counts. The ontology
therefore models structural form only, leaving flavour and nutrition aside.
2 Classes
2.1 Core Classes
Core Class Role Modelling Rationale
Bread Each individual slice of bread Counting how many slices are
associated with a sandwich lets one
infer structural types, open-faced,
standard or double-deckers, without
hard-coding those categories.
Filling Any edible item placed between (or
on) bread.
Detailed culinary taxonomies are
intentionally postponed so that future
extensions can plug in ingredient
ontologies as needed.
Deck A logical layer that groups fillings. Distinct deck instances make it
possible to reason about vertical
structure, such as layer counts or
repeated ingredients
SideDish Any food customarily served alongside
a sandwich.
Supports queries for typical
accompaniments without tying the
model to a particular vocabulary for
pairings.
Country Places where a sandwich style is
common.
It enables origin or regional popularity
queries without needing to build a
complete geopolitical ontology
Table 1: Core Classes
1

2.2 Subclasses
Subclass Hierarchical assertion
ToastedBread ⊑ Bread Bread denotes individual slices; “the bread may
be toasted before assembling”[1]. Toasted slices
inherit all axioms of Bread.
Open−, Toasted−, DoubleDecker−
Sandwich ⊑ Sandwich These are simple variants of the main class:
each inherits all axioms of Sandwich and is dis-
tinguished only by the slice count, layer ar-
rangement, or toasted state.
Table 2: Subclasses
3 Properties
There are six object-properties in the model.
• hasBreadSlice (Sandwich → Bread) — asymmetric. Containment cannot be re-
versible. A sandwich may have 1–3 slices; a bread individual might, in principle, be
referenced by two models.
• hasDeck (Sandwich → Deck) — asymmetric, inverse-functional. One-way con-
tainment again makes it asymmetric. A deck belongs to exactly one sandwich by defini-
tion, justifying inverse-functional.
• isFilledWith (Deck → Filling) — asymmetric. Fillings never contain their deck.
Multiple fillings per deck and possible reuse of a filling across sandwiches prohibit func-
tional or inverse-functional assertions.
• hasIngredient (Sandwich → Filling) — asymmetric and super-property. De-
fined by the chain
hasDeck ◦ isFilledWith ⊑ hasIngredient.
This allows ingredient facts to be inferred from layered data while still permitting direct
assertion when no Deck individuals are modelled. Direction remains one-way, so the link
is asymmetric.
• isCommonIn (Sandwich → Country) — asymmetric. Represents directional meta-
data (“Open sandwiches are common in Scandinavia”). The relation never operates in
reverse.
• servedWith (Sandwich ↔ SideDish) — symmetric. If a sandwich is served with
crisps, the crisps are served with that sandwich; reciprocity is inherent.
4 Axiom Definitions
4.1 Double-decker Sandwich
DoubleDeckerSandwich ≡ Sandwich ⊓
�
hasBreadSlice exactly 3 Bread

⊓
�
hasDeck exactly 2 Deck

2

English meaning: A double-decker sandwich is, by definition, a sandwich that contains three
slices of bread and two layers (decks) of filling. Source sentence: “A double decker sandwich
will have three slices of bread with two layers of fillings.”[1]
4.2 Open Sandwich
OpenSandwich ≡ Sandwich ⊓
�
hasBreadSlice exactly 1 Bread

⊓
�
hasDeck exactly 1 Deck

English meaning: An open sandwich is a sandwich made with one slice of bread and therefore
one deck of filling on top. Source sentence: “If there is only one piece of bread it is sometimes
called an open sandwich.”[1] Note: A plain slice of toast without any deck is therefore not a
sandwich.
4.3 Toasted Sandwich Constraint
ToastedSandwich ≡ Sandwich ⊓
�
hasBreadSlice some ToastedBread

English meaning: A toasted sandwich is any sandwich that includes at least one slice of
toasted bread. Source phrase: “Another form of sandwich is the toasted sandwich, where
the bread may be toasted before assembling . . . ”[1]
5 Advantages & Disadvantages
Beginning an ontology with the Simple-Wikipedia “Sandwich” entry combines clear practical
advantages with unavoidable drawbacks. It offers a solid foundation: because the article is
concise and community-reviewed, every concept can be verified manually, allowing the model
to scale quickly and safely. Its factual, openly licensed content also minimises the risk of
misinformation propagating through the ontology.
Nevertheless, three issues limit its usefulness. First, Simple-Wikipedia deliberately omits
fine-grained detail—cooking techniques, flavour profiles, and brand-specific variants are largely
absent. Second, the article’s perspective is implicitly Western; non-Western sandwiches may
be treated as entirely different foods rather than as members of the same category. Finally,
boundary definitions remain vague: edge cases such as hot-dogs or burritos are mentioned
without clear inclusion criteria, forcing individuals to create their own restrictions and proper-
ties. Hence, while the page is an excellent starting point, anyone aiming for a comprehensive,
complex ontology must enrich it with more specialised sources.

test and verify the correctness of ontology entities and property definitions created in Prot´ eg´ e.
